claims.claim: UN Tourism's IRTS 2008 defines a visitor as a traveler taking a trip to a main destination outside their usual environment, for less than a year, for any main purpose other than to be employed by a resident entity at the place visited.
A tourist is a visitor whose trip includes at least one overnight stay; a same-day visitor (excursionist) is a visitor whose trip does not include an overnight stay.
The 'usual environment' is the geographical area within which a person conducts their regular life routines; travel within it is not tourism.

IRTS 2008 names three basic forms against a country of reference: domestic tourism (resident visitor within the country), inbound tourism (non-resident visitor within the country), and outbound tourism (resident visitor outside the country); these combine into internal (domestic+inbound), national (domestic+outbound), and international (inbound+outbound) tourism.

Neil Leiper (1979) modeled tourism as a system of five elements: tourists, three geographical elements (traveller-generating region, transit route region, tourist destination region), and a tourist industry, joined by functional and spatial connections.

Leiper defined the generating region as the source of potential tourism demand and the place where trips begin and end; the destination region as locations that attract tourists to stay temporarily; the transit route as the region connecting the two through which tourists travel; and the tourist industry as the firms, organizations, and facilities intended to serve the specific needs and wants of tourists.

Leiper characterized tourism as an 'open system' and as only 'partially industrialized,' since much of what tourists use (public roads, scenery, hospitality from friends) is not provided by any tourism firm.

Tourism demand is commonly explained through push factors (internal motivations to leave home) and pull factors (a destination's attributes that attract travelers); Leiper cites Dann (1977) for the significance of push factors in generating regions.

Tourism supply is often analyzed with destination components whose names begin with 'A': a widely taught list (popularized by Dickman) is attractions, access, accommodation, amenities, and activities, while Buhalis (2000) uses six A's, adding ancillary services and available packages.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The exact membership of the 'A's' of tourism supply varies by author.
positions: Dickman's often-cited list: attractions, access, accommodation, amenities, activities (five A's).
Buhalis (2000): attractions, accessibility, amenities, available packages, activities, ancillary services (six A's).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the 'A's' as a widely taught framework, names attractions, access, accommodation, amenities, and ancillary services as the core, and states explicitly that the fifth 'A' varies by author, attributing both Dickman and Buhalis.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The full six-environment list (physical, cultural, social, economic, political, technological) surrounding Leiper's five elements is elaborated more fully in Leiper's later work (e.g., Leiper 1990 and his tourism-management texts) than in the 1979 paper.
positions: The 1979 paper establishes the five-element system and describes it as an 'open system.'
The named set of environments is the standard teaching elaboration of Leiper's model in later texts.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson attributes the five-element system and the 'open system' framing to Leiper's 1979 paper (read directly) and presents the environments as the teaching tradition built on Leiper's model, without over-claiming that all six terms appear verbatim in 1979.

sourceRecords.title: The Framework of Tourism: Towards a Definition of Tourism, Tourist, and the Tourist Industry
sourceRecords.provider: Neil Leiper, Annals of Tourism Research, 6(4), 390-407
sourceRecords.notes: Primary source for Leiper's tourism system. Read the full text directly from a publicly hosted PDF copy at https://franciscodosanjos.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/12/leiper.pdf (HTTP 200 via curl; text extracted from the PDF's zlib-compressed streams). Confirms the five elements (tourists; generating region as source of demand and start/end of trips; transit route connecting origin and destination; destination region as locations that attract tourists to stay temporarily; the tourist industry as firms/organizations/facilities intended to serve the specific needs and wants of tourists), the 'functional and spatial connections' across the system, the 'open system' framing, the 'partially industrialized' characteristic, the overnight-stay criterion demarcating tourists from day-trippers, and the citation of Dann (1977) for push factors. Copyrighted; reference-only, prose original. Canonical URL is the ScienceDirect DOI.
